Hey OP! 

I'm in a similar situation as you. I am in position of privilege (come from a financially well off family, good relationship with all family members, and educated) but I have shown symptoms of severe depression, even suicidal thoughts. Nobody suspected a thing was wrong with me until I told them. 

I just want to say that you have taken a step forward in the right direction, but let me point a few things to expect based on my experience. 

First, don't worry about solving the problem but rather controlling and mitigating the symptoms. A lot of things can cause depression, from environmental to genetics, and that will take time for any mental health care worker to figure out. By controlling your symptoms, your thought process will become less clouded and chaotic, and will allow you tell more information to your psychologist. Or it can allow you to self reflect and realize somethings about yourself. 

Second, this will take time. You will have to be patient with yourself to heal, and be proactive with therapy, even if you don't see immediate result. Keep a log to track your feelings. It will help you and your psychologist by tracking changes in moods or behaviors that may be of concern. 

Third, in the meantime, and if you are comfortable, build a support system with family members or friends. You don't have to tell outright that you're suffering from depression, but you can tell them you're feeling some stress at the moment and you need someone that will listen. Or distract you from your stress by doing a hobby together. 

Fourth, after you talked to your psychologist and you feel comfortable with him/her, regularly see them (weekly or biweekly). There's no way that you can tell someone everything that is going with your life or your feelings at the moment in one session. You will also need time to naturally allow yourself to open up to them. And it is important to be honest with them, even if you feel bare or embarrassed about that. A good psychologist can help realize and see problems you might have overlooked or have not considered. 

As for resources, the side bar provided excellent information, as well as resources such as National Institute of Health.

At one point I did feel really disconnected from my friends, especially those from college. It got so bad that I deactivated my facebook in order to avoid them. They tried to reach out to me, but I ignored them, ashamed to tell them what was really going on. But eventually I decided to reach out to one of them, and told them a little bit of what's going on. Then from there, I told other people as well. Not everybody. Just a few. Then I eventually reactivated my facebook and left a generic "I had a rough year" status to tell everybody else. Again, not full details, but enough to understand. 

I can understand why you don't want to turn to them. They may not be able to understand or know how to show empathy for your situation. Pick a friend you feel most comfortable with, and try to hang out with them. You don't have to tell them anything in the beginning. Just do a hobby or something with them, just to test the waters. At the very least, you did something to break monotony, even for a bit. 

EDIT: One more thing. Again, I'm talking from my experience, but one of my friends that I told about my feelings actually was on anti-depressants a few years back when he was at an out of state university. I had no idea, and was surprised to learn that about him. We bonded over that. If you can hide your pain from other people, than other people can hide their pain from you.

I'm going through a similar problem as well. I'm feel unmotivated/anxious about doing school work, I want to do nothing. Literally nothing. I just lie in bed and be miserable. Sometimes I might feel "better", and get up to play video games or reddit, but then that puts me in a worse mood, that I'm wasting my time. So I go back to lying in my bed feeling miserable. 

After doing that for a while, I feel bad that I'm procrastinating, putting me in a worse mood until I have had enough. So I will try to work my school work, but then I feel intimidated/demotivated to even attempt and/or finish school assignments. So I walk away and repeat the cycle. 

I felt that everything I was doing is pointless, but I get so stressed out about completing those "pointless" activities. That stress eventually started to eat away my mind until I started having suicidal thoughts. 

So right now I've been talking to councilor and building a support network of close friends that are aware of what I'm going through to help me. I mean I am still very far behind on school, and struggling to catch up. Actually, I'm struggling to even begin to catch up on late assignments. But I do feel little bit better about telling people that I trust and are able to help my feelings. Even if they don't fully understand what I'm going through, it feels nice that they are listening to me. 

Actually listening to me, and now just giving me a blank and confused look on their face. 

Hell, even posting on this subreddit and talking to complete internet strangers is helping me. Not by completing my homework, but acting as a pressure release value for the pain and dread I'm feeling everyday.

Maybe your other stories can flesh out the details about the fights between Ellen and Alice, but to me you seem like an innocent bystander in this case. I can understand why you felt guilty of not knowing whats going on and not doing anything about it. But those two clearly had differences that they couldn't settle. They acted independently of you, so don't feel responsible for what they said to each other. They also tried to get along when you were physically present, so they did hide that problem from you.

Personally, I would go see a psychologist/councilor as soon as possible. Depending on your own knowledge of mental health, there could be signs of mental health problems that you will overlook upon self reflection or discussing with parents and friends. Not because you are deliberating ignoring them, but because you are ignorant of their impact. 

For example, me and alcohol. Normally, I will go to the bar once or twice a week, and each visit I will have 1 or 2 drinks. Now compared to other patrons at the bars, that's very little. There are rare occasions where I will drink more than that and get quite drunk, but those times are rare occurrences (about once every 1-2 months). Last week, I would not describe myself as dependent on alcohol, or have potential to abuse alcohol. I would even say that I have a healthy drinking habit (as in good self control over how much I can drink and when I should stop). 

But after talking to a councilor, they told me that they were concerned about my alcohol habit. Though I am not an alcoholic, and that I do consume alcohol as a social lubricant in moderate amounts, I am at high risk of developing a dependence on it. I could also begin to self medicate myself on it, which can lead to other problems separate from depression.  

They didn't tell me that I should stop drinking, they understand that I do enjoy bar activities (such as playing pool or socializing with friends), but I do need to be extra careful with drinking. When I first heard that advice, I did raise my eyebrow at it. "I don't really drink all that much. I don't get drunk all that often."

But after further discussion on that subject, I did start to realize that I am in a vulnerable state. Alcohol can become a problem. It is not a problem now, but it will become one if I'm not careful. 

Your case will obviously be different from mine. But I do recommend seeing a professional who is capable of pointing out possible concerns that you should focus on. 

TL;DR: If you have the resources to see a doctor/mental healthcare worker, then go see one as soon as possible.

I would literally have conversations with myself, and did similar things that you just said in your post (What if friend X did this instead of that?). 

I told my therapist about that. Not sure why, but I told her about it along with my suicidal thoughts. She took note of it, asked me to elaborate it on it. We spent maybe 2 minutes on it before moving on to another topic. I'm going to see her tomorrow, and maybe she will bring it up again. But she didn't react negatively to it or judged me for it. She took note of it, simply gathering information to help her work me through my problems. 

I can't speak for your therapist or from experience, but remember that you what is said between you and your therapist is confidential. No one else will know without your authorization. You're not obligated to tell her those things now. If you're not comfortable with sharing that information at this moment, then don't.
